What structural ambiguity looks like in practice

Responsibility is unclear

Work may involve several teams without a shared understanding of who owns the next step. A specific example can help distinguish a missing responsibility from a communication issue.

Approval requirements are uncertain

A person may have formal authority but be unsure how it applies to a particular case. Reviewing the stated rule and a relevant example is more useful than assuming authority is absent.

Handoffs need clarification

A task may pass between several roles. The number of transfers alone does not show that any is unnecessary; the review should consider what each transfer contributes.

nformal coordination fills gaps

Meetings and informal conversations can help resolve uncertainty. A participant’s reliance on them is a reason to ask what needs clarification, not proof that the formal structure has failed.

Responsibilities when priorities change

Changing priorities can expose uncertainty about who should decide, act, or be consulted. Relevant work examples can help the responsible people review those boundaries.

Clear responsibilities are useful when they reflect the work people actually do. Any proposed change should preserve necessary approvals and be agreed by the responsible owner.
